profile.reading:
Lumen Technologies operates a colocation and network facility in downtown Baltimore, and the coordinates recorded for this entry point most consistently to 300 West Lexington Street, a roughly 33,000 square foot building a few blocks west of Baltimore's Inner Harbor and City Hall. Industry facility trackers and telecom carrier documentation associate that address with a data center formerly branded under Level 3 Communications, the long haul network operator Lumen absorbed in 2017 when CenturyLink acquired Level 3, with the combined company renaming itself Lumen Technologies in 2020. Lumen's own public materials describe its national edge cloud and colocation portfolio in general terms without publishing a street address, floor plan, or capacity figure for the Baltimore location specifically, so this entry's address should be read as well supported by coordinate proximity and industry directories rather than confirmed directly by an operator statement.

Downtown Baltimore has a small cluster of similar telecom facilities within a few blocks of each other, reflecting the city's history as a mid Atlantic long distance and fiber interconnection point going back to the Bell System and C&P Telephone era, and the building at 300 West Lexington fits that pattern as a converted or purpose adapted telecom facility rather than new construction built for a single hyperscale tenant. No source found in this research gives a year built, floor count, or ownership history for this specific address, and no critical IT load, utility power figure, standby generation rating, or onsite generation figure could be attributed to it from any primary source located during this pass. Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation records and Baltimore City property records were not consulted directly and would be the logical next step to confirm ownership and improved square footage independent of the figures carried in telecom industry directories.

What can be said with confidence is that this is a network centric colocation site rather than a hyperscale campus, that it sits inside Lumen's broader edge and interconnection strategy for the mid Atlantic, and that Lumen Technologies itself is the successor entity to CenturyLink, Qwest, and Level 3 Communications, three companies whose networks were consolidated over roughly two decades of mergers. What is not known, and is flagged here rather than guessed at, is the building's exact power capacity, its tenancy beyond Lumen, and whether Lumen leases space inside a larger multi tenant building or occupies it outright.

reading.body:
Lumen Baltimore is a network colocation facility at 300 West Lexington Street in downtown Baltimore, operated by Lumen Technologies as part of its mid-Atlantic edge cloud portfolio. The building is a converted or adapted telecom property rather than new construction, reflecting Baltimore's century-long role as a long distance and fiber interconnection hub. Lumen publishes no IT load, power capacity, or floor count for this specific location.

The facility's power consumption and rack density are not published. Without those figures, this campus cannot be translated into equivalent AI accelerators or training clusters. It sits within a small cluster of similar network-centric colocation sites in downtown Baltimore, built or repurposed for carrier equipment rather than hyperscale compute, and predates current public debate over data center power draw in Maryland.

Maryland has 11 mapped data center facilities and only 3 with published capacity totaling 9.3 MW. Lumen Baltimore ranks fourth in the state by published megawatts, which is zero. This facility matters to AI infrastructure only to the degree that Lumen's interconnection points and edge colocation capabilities feed hyperscale cloud tenants elsewhere. Its own capacity contribution to AI scaling cannot be measured from available data.
